intro.caption: Lesson 5-10 — volume of rectangular prisms. Market Day in Cubeland! Moss's new plaza sandbox has a fractional height, and Dree just dropped the fraction from the order!

balloons.t: Our sandbox is 4 ft long, 3 ft wide, and 1½ ft tall. How much sand fills it?
I can help! I already ate the order slip!
Fractions are annoying, so I dropped the ½! 4 × 3 × 1 = 12 cubic feet!
Wait! Estimate first! 1½ is halfway between 1 and 2, so 12 ft³ is way too small!

pages.caption: Never drop a fractional edge! Estimate first using the whole numbers below and above the fraction to catch a short order.

balloons.t: Bracket 1½ between 1 and 2. Where must the real volume land?
A fractional edge does not change the rule! Find the base area first, then multiply by height.
Base area = 4 × 3 = 12 ft². Stack that 1½ times high!
Don't guess by height alone! Multiply all three dimensions to compare crates.
And multiply 3 × 2.5—never add them by mistake!
Pick the wrong bin and your sandbox stays half empty!
We need at least 5 cubic feet. Let's compute every bin and pick the winner!
Six cubic feet! Enough sand for a cube castle!

win.caption: To find the volume of a rectangular prism—even with fractional edges—multiply length × width × height or base area × height, and label in cubic units.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Estimate First
gates.prompt: Estimate the volume of the 4 ft × 3 ft × 1½ ft sandbox before computing, so you never drop the ½.
hints: Conceptual: 1½ is greater than 1 and less than 2, so the volume must fall between using 1 and using 2.
Procedural: compute the low bound (4 × 3 × 1) and the high bound (4 × 3 × 2).

steps: Low bound (using 2): 5 × 2 × 2 = 20 ft³. High bound (using 3): 5 × 2 × 3 = 30 ft³.
Since 2½ is halfway between 2 and 3, the volume is between 20 and 30 ft³.
worked.q: For a 3 × 2 × 1½ box, what two whole-number volumes does the answer sit between?

items.q: The sandbox is 4 ft × 3 ft × 1½ ft. Dree drops the ½ and guesses 12 ft³. Which estimate range is right?

options.t: Between 12 ft³ and 24 ft³, because 1½ is between 1 and 2
Exactly 12 ft³, because ½ is too small to matter
options.fb: Half of a 4 × 3 layer is 6 extra cubic feet—a huge amount to drop!
1½ is bigger than 1, so the volume must be MORE than 4 × 3 × 1 = 12.
Even at height 2 ft, 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 ft³, so it cannot be over 30.

items.label: What is the upper whole-number bound 4 × 3 × 2 (ft³)?
items.aria: upper estimate 4 times 3 times 2 in cubic feet

fb.msg: 12 is 4 × 3 × 1 (the lower bound). Use height 2 for the upper bound.

gates.pass: Between 12 and 24 ft³! Now Dree knows 12 ft³ would leave the sandbox half empty.

gates.title: Gate 2 · Base Area Times Height
gates.prompt: Find the base area B = l × w first, then multiply by the fractional height 1½ ft.
hints: Conceptual: V = B × h stacks the flat base layer up to the height, even when the height has a fraction.
Procedural: multiply 12 × 1½ by splitting it into (12 × 1) + (12 × ½).

worked.q: A box has base area 8 ft² and height 1.5 ft. What is its volume?

items.label: For the 4 ft × 3 ft × 1½ ft sandbox, what is the base area B = 4 × 3 (ft²)?
items.aria: base area 4 times 3 in square feet

fb.msg: 14 is the perimeter 2(4 + 3). Base area is length × width.

items.label: Now multiply base area 12 ft² by height 1.5 ft. Exact volume (ft³):
items.aria: exact volume 12 times 1.5 in cubic feet

fb.msg: 12 dropped the ½! Add 12 × ½ = 6 to 12.
8.5 added 4 + 3 + 1.5. Volume multiplies all three dimensions.

gates.pass: 18 ft³—right halfway between 12 and 24! Kai stacks the half-layer on top.

gates.title: Gate 3 · Compare the Crates
gates.prompt: Compute the volume of a decimal-edge crate and compare two storage crates at the market.
hints: Conceptual: volume multiplies all three dimensions (never add two edges), and taller does not always mean bigger volume.
Procedural: multiply l × w × h for each crate, then compare the cubic totals.

steps: Practice crates: Crate X is 3 × 2 × 2.5 = 15 ft³. Crate Y is 4 × 2 × 2 = 16 ft³.
Even though Crate X is taller (2.5 > 2), Crate Y holds more because 16 > 15.
worked.q: What is the volume of a 6 × 2 × 1.5 box?

items.label: A market crate is 5 m × 3 m × 2.5 m. Volume (m³):
items.aria: volume of 5 by 3 by 2.5 meter crate in cubic meters

fb.msg: 27.5 added 3 + 2.5 = 5.5, then multiplied by 5! Multiply 3 × 2.5 = 7.5 first.
30 dropped the 0.5! Include the full 2.5 m height.

items.q: Crate A is 5 × 5 × 2 in and Crate B is 4 × 4 × 3 in. Which crate holds more?

options.t: Crate B, because it is taller (3 in > 2 in)
options.fb: Height alone doesn't decide volume! Crate B is 4 × 4 × 3 = 48 in³, while Crate A is 5 × 5 × 2 = 50 in³.

options.t: Crate A, because 50 in³ is greater than 48 in³

options.fb: 5 × 5 × 2 = 50 in³, while 4 × 4 × 3 = 48 in³. They are close, not equal.

gates.pass: 37.5 m³ and Crate A (50 in³ > 48 in³)! Moss picks the winner.

gates.title: Boss Gate · Place the Order
gates.prompt: Three bins at the market: Small (2 × 1 × 1 ft), Medium (2 × 1.5 × 1 ft), and Large (2 × 2 × 1.5 ft). The plaza needs at least 5 ft³.
hints: Conceptual: multiply all three edges for each bin, keeping every fractional part, then compare to 5 ft³.
Procedural: find V = l × w × h for the Medium bin and the Large bin, then choose the bin ≥ 5 ft³.

worked.q: What is the volume of a 4 × 1.5 × 2 bin?

items.label: Medium bin is 2 ft × 1.5 ft × 1 ft. Volume (ft³):
items.aria: volume of Medium bin 2 by 1.5 by 1 in cubic feet

items.label: Large bin is 2 ft × 2 ft × 1.5 ft. Volume (ft³):
items.aria: volume of Large bin 2 by 2 by 1.5 in cubic feet

items.q: The plaza needs at least 5 ft³ of sand. Which bin should the crew buy?

options.fb: 2 ft³ is less than 5 ft³—way too small.
3 ft³ is still under the 5 ft³ needed.

options.t: Large bin (6 ft³), the only one that holds at least 5 ft³

gates.pass: POUR! Medium = 3 ft³, Large = 6 ft³—order placed! The sandbox fills right to the top.

journal.heading: Lesson 5-10 — what the block market taught us
rows: Fractional edges do not change the formula: V = length × width × height, or V = base area × height.
Use the whole numbers below and above a fraction to bracket the volume and catch mistakes.
Volume measures 3D space inside a solid, so answers use cubic units (ft³, in³, m³).
Dropping the ½ from 1½ loses half a layer! Always multiply the full mixed number or decimal.
journal.quote: "Never drop the half—unless it's half a blueprint near Gel." — Ana

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 5-10 (Volume of Rectangular Prisms) as one focused read. Covers only this lesson: estimating and computing volume of rectangular prisms with whole and fractional edge lengths using V = l × w × h and V = B × h.
standards: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with fractional edge lengths
